utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we admit part of the transcript yesterday or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We didn't, Your Honour, because the -- because most of the propositions that were put to Mr. Banduka he accepted that this relates to two propositions that he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll admit those three pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit P6110. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, yesterday on page 84 of the transcript you were asked about the attack on Hadzici of the 11th of May. utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, on the 11th of May an attack took place in the early morning hours on Hadzici from Tinovo Brdo and from Vrbanja. So that was a Muslim attack which resulted in a number of fatalities on our side and it was repelled on that same day, but I'm not aware of any attack on Musici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 25594 dated 11th of May, 1995 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 24594.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, let's look at paragraph 1. Here the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina reports on the 11th of May that at around 25 minutes after midnight there was a renewed attack on Serb positions. Do you see this first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with what you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put a pause between the question and the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably my question was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This speaks about a renewed attack on the 11th after midnight, that the technical depot was targeted as well as the public security station. Is that consistent with what you know about this attack?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this renewed attack? When did the attacks that preceded this one occur?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an attack on the 10th of May. You saw in my statement that on the 10th of May the Muslims seized the barracks in Krupska Rijeka and also the Serbs' part were shelled, the Serb parts of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit D2921, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often and what was the intensity of the shelling targeting the centre part of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the shelling of the central part of Hadzici and the neighbouring villages were a daily occurrence. Let me tell you just that on 25th of May, when there was a major attack by the Muslim forces, 10 or 11 of our troops were killed and eight of them were killed by shelling. In other words, shelling was happening on a daily basis from Igman, from village of Lokve, and Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would this correspond to D2469, where you say that on one day 27 shells landed and another day 117 shells, including Weber rockets, and they hit the centre of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am able to remember and according to what was recorded, I think that the fiercest shelling was on the 5th or 6th of June when the Muslim forces took over the Pazarici barracks, albeit through negotiations. There were about some 100 troops there and a large amount of heavy weapons. And we estimated that on that very same day over 1.000 shells fell on Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is relating to a telephone conversation between Lieutenant-Colonel Milicevic and General Mladic which took place on the 21st. Who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30789.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may, this line of questioning has continued for some time and I fail to see how this flows from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, yesterday the Prosecution refuted the development of events, whereas Mr. Banduka said that we were being shelled on a daily basis. And whatever was happening was happening during the shelling. This opened the door for this subject in cross-examination as to whether they had weapons, who went there of their own volition, who was detained in the sports centre and the garages. All of this was raised as a result of the questions put by the Prosecution and the things happening in Dupovac, Musici, et cetera, even 92 quater which is something that I am not in a position to put questions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you meant by saying that Prosecution refuted the development of events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, yesterday the Prosecution said on page 84 of the transcript, they denied the claim that it was the Muslims who attacked Hadzici and they referred to Witness Music and the others, and they claim that this was, in fact, done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was also mention of the sports hall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether she made a claim denying Muslim attacks at all, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could be directed to a specific transcript reference, that would be helpful because that claim wasn't made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll wait until we find this transcript page, but everything else that was contained in Music's testimony was made reference to and I need to clarify that. Mr. Banduka gave the same response as Music did. So the whole issue was raised yesterday during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She raised -- she put some questions with respect to -- or in relation to Music's statement. As far as the item is related to those parts, you may proceed. But by putting certain paragraph in the Music's statement, it does not open the door for everything that is contained in his statement. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. While we are waiting can we -- oh, yes, now we have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, can you see here what it says, I am the commander?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Pazarici unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we check -- yes, it says here Hadzici municipality. But now we need to go to the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain first how this relates to Ms. McKenna's cross-examination of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot give the exact reference but there was a dispute that they were well-armed. However, they took over the barracks that was fully loaded with arms and immediately thereafter they launched an attack on Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She did ask about the Serbs arming, but I'm not sure she challenged or she disputed the Muslim -- the arming on the part of the Muslim side at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 87 the witness said that as soon as the Muslims had left Hadzici of their own volition, it was followed by an attack on the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 33477. Does that mean that somebody was bringing them in or did they arrive of their own volition? Is it -- is this the part you are referring to? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I don't have that number, or rather, these final numbers in LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, could you read the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please have it on the screen, that page, because I can't find it because I don't have numbers like that. I'll try. I do apologise. I'll try to find it according to my own numbers because I don't have those numbers. Sixteen, 17, and 18 are the lines in yesterday's transcript. I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Q. Mr. Banduka, I'm going to move on to the topic of the Hadzici sports centre. At paragraph 54 of your statement you say that: 'The Crisis Staff set up a clothing centre in the sports hall, seeing that the remaining Muslim inhabitants were complaining every day that they were experiencing ...'" And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Page 33510, page 33510.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us take a look at page 74. According to my numbering, lines 22 through 25. In the question it says: [In English] "Well, Mr. Dupovac who actually attended the council, his evidence was that the SDS didn't refuse to participate in the functions of the council until mid-April. And, in fact, they used the Defence Council as platform to emphasise their desire for Muslims and Serbs to have separate state. Mr. Banduka, did you -- were you aware of the SDS making public statements about the desire for Muslims and Serbs to have separate states?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: For Your Honours' reference, that's page 33497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But once again, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 87 there's another reference to Dupovac and I could not cross-examine. 33498 is the page number, lines 5 to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So again this was related to the arming on the part of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here on page 74 it says -- I'll read it out. The question was: [In English] "You said that they had already informed their units. Now earlier today you removed a reference in your statement to the Serbs making preparations in war ..." and so on. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, there is total chaos as far as page numbers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found it. It's 33498. Yes, court deputy pointed out already. It's all related to the arming on the part of the Serbs. The Defence -- the Prosecution didn't challenge the arming on the part of the Muslims if I remember correctly. Instead of using your precious time, I would like you to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to draw your attention to the answer on the next page, the first line, where Mr. Banduka says that they were the ones who had been attacked on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, now we're going to abandon that topic all together. Tell me, please, what was the attitude of the authorities towards the Muslim in Hadzici, in the Serb part of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the attitude was the way it was towards all the inhabitants of Hadzici. There was no difference, starting with ordinary things, because we had enormous problems with water-supply, power-supply, food supplies, so everybody was in the same position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2306, that's what I'd like to draw the attention of the participants to and I'm going to read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A report on the work of the Serb municipality of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Members of other ethnic groups live in this municipality on the condition that they accept the constitutional order of Republika Srpska. The members of the Assembly said that this has to ensure the equality of rights of Serbs and other citizens living in the area. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to what you know regarding the attitude towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is a Prosecution document. Yesterday you asserted that the Muslim civilians left and that attack ensued; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music who was mentioned here, mentioned by the Prosecution, he also confirmed that buses arrived and that they drove civilians towards Pazarici and that he was even in charge of the evacuation of these civilians. Did you know Mr. Mehmed Music?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That Prosecution report was for 1992, I mean 2306. Yesterday when asked whether there were prisoners in the sports hall, you said that that could have been the case only if they were released from custody that was actually detention in the municipality building. Is that what you say today as well?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Music said on page 132 of his amalgamated statement: [In English] "If a person was presumed to be guilty, the prisoner would be held at the garage; otherwise, they would be taken to sports hall." [Interpretation] Do you say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Yesterday the Prosecution asked me about this. Yes, these persons who were in the garages had been brought into custody, but there were Serbs among them as well, persons who had committed crimes. People who were stealing the property of other people, people who were shooting, firing weapons, they were brought into custody to the garage and that's where they were interrogated as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 152 of his amalgamated statement

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSIC SAYS
utterances.text: [In English] "The people who continued to be held at the municipality building were involved in more serious cases." [Interpretation] What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I said. They were transferred to the Kula prison as soon as that was possible so that they could be prosecuted by the authorities that are in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when questioned about civilians at the sports hall you said that that could happen only if they were returned from unsuccessful exchanges. Then as they waited for an exchange they would stay at the sports hall. Can you tell us what that means, unsuccessful exchange, and how could civilians actually get there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exchanges were organised predominantly through Croatian territory. Actually, our neighbouring municipality was Kiseljak and primarily through the mediation of Croats at the border crossing of Kobiljaca, that's what we called it, that's where these agreed exchanges would take place between the representatives of the Serbs and the representatives of the Muslims. As far as I know there were even direct contacts between certain families. So there were large-scale exchanges that took place. People were transferred by bus to the point where the exchanges were being organised, but for a variety of reasons these exchanges would fail. There would be problems, technical problems, or there would be strings attached, especially the Muslim side was always putting forth condition. So we had no other way of dealing with this situation but keeping them at the sports hall until a successful exchange were to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you quoted two parts from Mr. Music's amalgamated statement. You said one is from page 132 and the other from paragraph 152, but I couldn't find those pages -- either in terms of page number or in terms of para numbers. Could you give the reference again. As I see it, the last paragraph number is 133.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it right now, Excellency. I think that it was referred to in the transcript as well. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Ms. McKenna can find the reference, if you could let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The reference is 152. That's what I have here, and the paragraph is 52 in the statement. That's the first reference. I do apologise. I was reading my own footnotes. I was reading them out as if they were paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see the quote, para 52. Let's continue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, Mr. Music in his statement says that he tried seven times to exchange his own family and that it failed six times and then the seventh time the exchange succeeded. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe the statement because, as I said previously, that kind of thing did happen. There were a great many obstructions from the Muslim side. So everything was agreed upon until the exchange was supposed to take place, and then they invented all sorts of problems. I know about that. That made our work a lot more difficult. This was terrible pressure that was exerted on the municipal organs, to exchange these people who were at the Silo camp and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Banduka, can you just explain another thing to us: How were these lists created, lists of people who were supposed to leave? Was that based on their own wishes? And how were they informed that a bus was ready? If you were not involved in this, never mind, you don't have to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't involved, but as I've already said I did know. Usually through mediation. It was the Croats who were allowed access to both the Serb and the Muslim sides, and they would bring information and take information. I remember this one particular case, it had to do with some close relatives of my late sister-in-law and I went to Kobiljaca, and I was an eye-witness to the fact that this Muslim brought this Serb family and he asked me to help bring his family there, that is to say his wife and children. And of course we went out, brought his family, and the exchange took place right there and then. So these exchanges were agreed upon in the different ways, and later on it was the commission on exchanges that primarily dealt with the matter. To tell you the truth, I don't even know who established these commissions. Were they state commissions? I don't know but the anyway, they compiled lists, they were involved in communications, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the municipality? The municipal authorities, did they have mechanisms in place that would force civilians to leave Hadzici, civilians to leave Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't have any mechanisms nor did they use them, and as a result many Muslims remained in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Banduka. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] it wasn't recorded fully. The witness said: Many Muslims remained in Hadzici throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One sentence only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what is it about? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to comment yesterday's questioning. When the Prosecutor mentioned the sports hall, she mentioned the date of 25th of May when allegedly forces burst into that facility and tortured the prisoners. I would like to say that by the 25th of May we had 26 dead men, ages between 20 and 70, including civilians. So if somebody slapped somebody on the face, but I can categorically say that every last man left the sports hall completely unscathed. However, people who were incarcerated in the Silo, I'm talking about the Serb people, were tortured and killed simply because of the truth and for the sake of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna, would you like to ask further questions with respect to this comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution notification and request relative to notice of disclosure of translation of report of Stevo Pasalic, filed on the 14th of December, 2012, to which I will refer here after as "request." In the request, the Prosecution first submits that while it does not challenge Stevo Pasalic's qualifications as an expert in demographics, it does not accept the conclusions in the expert report tendered pursuant to Rule 94 bis; second, in the Prosecution request the opportunity to cross-examine him; and third, it requests that the Chamber not admit annex A of the expert report. The Prosecution contends that annex A of the report contains Pasalic's findings relating to the suffering of Serbs and Serb villages between 1992 and 1995 which are irrelevant to the crimes charged in the indictment and the alleged criminal liability of the accused in this case. The accused did not respond to the request. The Chamber considers that the information contained in annex A to the report relates to detailed statistics relating to the "suffering of the Serbs and Serbian settlements" in municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina or BiH during the war, some of which have no geographical relevance to this case, and as such, is no different from the information which in the Chamber's practice has been excluded on the ground that it is detailed tu quoque evidence and not relevant to the charges in the indictment. The Chamber therefore grants the request and shall exclude annex A, namely, pages 69 through 102 of Pasalic's expert report. A redacted version of the report should be uploaded onto e-court prior to the start of Mr. Pasalic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That said, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Celikovic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Celikovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us pause between questions and answers and let us speak slowly so that everything can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have 1D7207 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celikovic, do you see the statement before you? Is that the statement that you gave to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have the last page for you to identify your signature.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it on the 10th of February, 2013. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement and does it reflect exactly what you said?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as posed by the Defence team, would you basically give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would completely give identical answers as I did in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read Mr. Savo Celikovic's summary statement in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I take it the Defence is not tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D2922. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the summary in English. [In English] Savo Celikovic was born on 9th February, 1952, in Vlasenica. He completed the primary school in Vlasenica and he graduated from the secondary school and then from the faculty of mechanical engineering in Sarajevo. In 1976, he took up employment at the Boksit mine in Vlasenica. In 1987 he was elected president of the Vlasenica municipality Assembly for a one-year term of office. After the multi-party elections were conducted in Vlasenica, he was elected to the municipality Assembly as a member of SDP party, left party, leftist party. On 21st of April, 1992, he was mobilised in the TO -- Territorial Defence as a logistical support officer, later in the Sekovici Brigade and then in the Milici and Vlasenica Brigade. When Mr. Savo Celikovic worked at the Alpro factory, the enterprise was ethnically mixed, the production ran smoothly, and there were no interethnic problems. The situation in Vlasenica became more complicated after the Muslims killed a Serbian employee of the Boksit mine as well as ambushing and killing drivers from the mine. They also killed a Serb who was a deputy of the National Assembly. The population of Vlasenica panicked and both Serbs and Muslims left in droves, and after this many Muslims no longer reported for work but were not fired. After the multi-party elections, Savo Celikovic was elected to the municipality on the list of SDP. As I said, the power in the Assembly was shared by the SDA, the SDS, and the SDP, and Alliance for the Reform Forces. From the beginning he found that the work of the Assembly was difficult because of the frequent disagreements between the Muslims and Serbs and there was not much progress. In mid-1991 the rising ethnic tensions brought on fear among both Serbs and Muslims and therefore night watches were organised in the villages. These were initially mixed watches; however, due to the growing distrust they became separate. Savo Celikovic was called up in mid-1991 in Han Pijesak, 216th Brigade. He was aware that the reason for the call-up was to prepare the troops for combat-readiness. Due to the conflicts in Croatia their presence was to try to prevent war in Bosnia. After a few days of training buses arrived of training close to the Banja -- in [indiscernible] Banja Luka. Buses arrived carrying SDA leaders and the president of the municipality, who was the Muslim from the SDA. The leaders of SDA addressed the soldiers and called upon the Muslims in the units to leave the JNA immediately and return home. The unit was also addressed by a battalion commander and a reservist who asked the Muslims not to listen to the SDA leaders. The reservist was of Muslim ethnicity. However, many Muslims left the unit after this and soon after the unit was sent home and Savo Celikovic returned to work. Further training was carried out in 1991 and in 1992 -- and in 1992 the Territorial Defence began to mobilise soldiers. Towards the end of 1991 or early 1992 an idea was debated in the Vlasenica Municipal Assembly for the municipality of Vlasenica to join the SAO, Serbian Autonomous Region, Birac. The reason for this was the fear of war as it was clear that the Muslims wanted to create a Muslim sovereign state. After this decision was adopted an initiative was launched in order to preserve the peace in Vlasenica. The idea was to divide the territory into three municipalities which was adopted. No one was threatened in the process of this decision being made and many agreed this solution was better than war. The Vlasenica Territorial Defence was mobilised on the 21st of April, 1992, and tasked with preventing any sabotage attack on public institutions or enterprises of public interest. During the night there were sporadic shooting incidents, mostly in mono-ethnic villages. Many more residents began leaving Vlasenica and around this time Serbs who had been expelled from surrounding villages began arriving in Vlasenica demanding to be housed. The authorities had already formed commissions that went around the town and sealed homes and flats of Muslims who had left, so that their property would not be stolen. A commission was formed to assign houses for the Serbian refugees' temporary use. To prevent the Muslim population from experiencing stress and mistreatment, the municipal authority decided to turn to the -- the Territorial Defence facilities into a reception -- in Susica into a reception centre for Serbs, and later on Muslims in Vlasenica could be housed in order to protect them from mistreatment or possible physical attacks. Prior to this, the facilities had been used as a reception centre for Serb -- for the Serb refugees. When the municipal authorities offered the remaining Muslim population temporary accommodation, the majority of the Muslims accepted it. The formation of the paramilitary groups the Patriotic League was an open secret because it was discussed every day in the town. In the front lines in Vlasenica in the beginning of 1992 were formed spontaneously when the Serbian and Muslim populations relocated on their own initiative and settled the villages where they were the majority. The lines remained pretty much unchanged until the end of war demonstrating that the war was defensive. In early May 1992 the Muslims started attacking the Serbian villages which they mainly torched and destroyed, killing locals and looting their property. The Serb army did not attack Muslim villages, it only defended its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was the summary, Mr. Celikovic. Would you be so kind as to tell me since we had a witness here who spoke about cash, can you tell us which currency was in circulation in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the currency was the dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat. We did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose dinars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What currency was in circulation in Vlasenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time that was the dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yugoslav dinar?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the laws were still in force of the federal state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How was your financial situation regarding cash and how did you obtain cash, from where?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly during that period the economy was still operating, all the enterprises were working, and up until May when due to a deterioration of the political security situation, a considerable portion of both the Serb and Muslim populations left town. It was unavoidable to suspend the operation because, quite simply, the majority of people who were fit for work failed to show up at work and fulfil their obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have noted, Mr. Celikovic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted into evidence in most part in writing instead of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Celikovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're going to start by discussing some items that are not in your statement. There was a period of time after 1995 when you served as president of the Executive Board of Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were removed from that position on the 29th of November, 1999, by the Office of the High Representative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And that decision banned you from being a candidate in the next municipal elections and banned you from holding any executive office at any level; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And one of the findings of that decision was that you abused your power by persistently and seriously obstructing the implementation of the General Framework Agreement for Peace, that you pursued an extra-legal agenda, and consistently refused to take ownership of the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, actually let's look at 65 ter number 24600, if we could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I think the witness should be given a chance to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course. He can comment after having taken a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see that this is a copy of the decision we're discussing from the 29th of November, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you'll have a look at the first three lines under "reasons for removal," it says: "Mr. Savo Celikovic has abused his power by persistently and seriously obstructing the implementation of the General Framework Agreement for Peace. By pursuing an extra-legal agenda, he has consistently refused to take ownership of the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: How about a translation of this decision so that I would be reminded?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a translation for you, but I just read the text for you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, may I explain then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is a fact that in that period of time, 1998, I was president of the Executive Board and the Executive Board consisted of either five or six members. Among them, there was an equitable member of the Muslim people who did not live in Vlasenica. From time to time he would come to attend sessions once he received the documents for the session involved. It is a fact that in that period of time of reconstruction and development, the Executive Board worked in accordance with the statute of the municipality of Vlasenica and the laws that were in force, the laws of Republika Srpska, or rather, in accordance with the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In its work during that period of time, when the economy was supposed to get started again, when displaced persons and refugees were supposed to be taken care of as well, also the gradual return of the population that had fled was supposed to be organised too. There was still a lack of trust and a lack of security as far as returns were concerned. We resolved these matters together to everyone's satisfaction. From time to time, when there was certain problems - the international community held this against me, as a matter of fact -- and one of these issues was the use of abandoned Bosniak property and freeing this property of the persons who were using it. I'm sorry. We, in the Executive Board, established a commission for the return of property. And on behalf of the Executive Board a person who had a degree in law was on this commission - this person had worked in various judiciary institutions for many years and other institutions in Sarajevo - he had fled to Vlasenica because he was a local person and he was the member of this commission and then also the head for town planning was also a member on behalf of the Executive Board. He was a professional who was well-versed in these matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Celikovic, if I could ask you to pause for a moment. I would like you to focus your attention on the four points that are listed in the document which relate in part to what you've been discussing about this establishment of a Property Commission. What the document says is in the first point that you were extremely uncooperative and refusing to meet to discussing the establishment of the Property Commission. The second point says that you finally accepted the establishment of the Property Commission under the condition that two members be appointed by yourself. It goes on to say in the third point that these two members repeatedly intervened with the work of the OMI on evictions and made a number of covert threats, and that this was particularly ominous in view of the subsequently violent attacks aimed at the OMI officer. And finally, that the municipality has passed a number of discriminatory administrative tax laws, that when you were confronted with that issue by the international community, you admitted that those laws were designed to penalise Bosniaks and in spite of your agreement to have those repealed, that had yet to happened. Can I ask you, the OMI is the ministry of refugees and displaced persons, which was tasked with allowing people to move back into their property; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: I just have to respond to the previous question. I need to finish by saying what the reasons were for which I thought that I should not be on that commission myself. Since this was a commission that worked in an operative fashion and practically it was supposed to visit abandoned properties every day and propose laws and different measures, at the time when I talked to different representatives I said, quite literally: Do you think that it is more urgent to be on that commission or should certain members of the commission propose measures and should the Executive Board headed by myself work out adequate solutions and take measures? That is one of the questions involved. The second one that has to do with certain taxes, it is a fact that these taxes were somewhat different and that is something that I inherited, if you will, that is to say when I came to the Executive Board. But it is also a fact that in that immediate period there were some wheelers and dealers, especially from the Muslim side and they, in fact, took large commissions for themselves when mediating for such exchanges and documents. For example, they would take commissions of 100 to 200 marks per document. We launched this initiative at the Executive Board at the proposal of the Bosniak member and we made a proposal to the Assembly. For certain reasons, for a while the Assembly could not meet. So the Assembly did not adopt these amendments, these amended taxes, that is to say aimed at preventing discrimination. That is to say that the Executive Board did make certain efforts, but it is really within the scope of the authority of the Assembly to adopt all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document into evidence, and I would note that the ERN is still being obtained. So we will substitute the document with an ERN'd one once it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your ERN comment. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're waiting to give -- to have an ERN -- or ERNs put on the pages of the document. So we'll tender the document into evidence but we'll have to replace it with an ERN'd version once it's ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Aha. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P6111. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Celikovic, after this removal from office you later ran for election and were elected as a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS party in Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not run for election. I was still a member of the Serb Democratic Party and I remained one until I was replaced, but to this day I don't know the true reasons for my dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, you were a member of the Municipal Board of the party; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were removed from that position as well on 30 June 2004, again by the Office of the High Representative?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I'm a unique case and having been dismissed twice, and to this day I don't know the true reasons for my dismissal. But in the interest of the party as well, I accepted that and I was no longer active in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, this removal prevented you from being active in the party; correct? It removed you from your position, it barred you from holding official elective or appointed office, it banned you from running in elections, and it banned you from holding office in any political party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is correct, but my constitutional rights had been violated in terms of having the right to vote and to be elected. However, very fortunately I have a degree in engineering and I worked as an engineering, I worked as a professional, and that had nothing to do with the Office of the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, you say that your rights had been violated, although you were part of a lawsuit against the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to try to reverse that decision and that went to the European Court of Human Rights and you lost; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you never know. I think that sooner rather than later justice will prevail and that evidence will become relevant. Perhaps at that point in time there was no adequate evidence. It is a fact that a few of us handed this case to the law team of Mr. Cavoski. He represented us. But I do know that we lost our case, but we are going to seek justice and this will yield results eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: There's no -- in this case there's no need to seek justice because that decision was repealed. The decision of the office of the high representative was repealed with the arrest of Ratko Mladic in 2011; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what was written in the decision, but the reasons for dismissing me were untrue, what was stated then. As for the president, I didn't even know him and least of all could I contribute in any way to these allegations that were referred to in the decision on my dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to your witness statement. And paragraph 18 you say, and I quote: "Towards the end of 1991 or early in 1992, an idea was launched in the Vlasenica Municipal Assembly for the municipality of Vlasenica to join the region SAO Serbian Autonomous District, Birac District. By this time Bratunac and Sekovici had already adopted a decision to join. The reason for joining these municipalities was the fear of war, because it was clear that the Muslims wanted a war in order to create a sovereign Muslim state." Now, was this a spontaneous decision or was this encouraged by higher authorities with the goal of creating a Serbian Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This has to do with that decision. Actually, before this decision in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina a decision was passed, or rather, a declaration was passed on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was passed by two peoples, or rather, the representatives of the Croat and Muslim peoples at the expense of the Serb people, and a decision was made to have a referendum held. The Serb people in the area of Birac had bad experience from the past. They were victims in the past. Quite simply, they were afraid of being out-voted. Otherwise, in the previous period there were these economic, educational, and cultural ties. So in addition to the fact that we used to belong to Tuzla as some kind of administrative centre, it was Zvornik that was the centre of the region. For that reason, we believed that such an autonomous region would ensure certain guarantees and rights so that we could protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, wasn't --

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] pardon me. Wasn't one of the reasons for joining that it was part of a Serb national goal to establish Serb control over territory that was leading all the way to the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We, especially the members of the Assembly, who were there representing the alliance for a reformed Yugoslavia from the SDP, that is to say there were three of us who were not of the same ethnicity, we were nostalgic and we advocated the following: That we should remain within Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia. That is one of the reasons why before the Assembly we launched this idea, namely --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: May I just -- may I just clarify one point of this which is you are speaking as a member of the SDP at this point. You're not speaking on behalf of the intentions of the SDS at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. At the time the representatives of the SDS -- well, it is a fact that there was this proposal to call it the SAO Birac, the Serb Autonomous Region of Birac. And it was precisely for the reason that I mentioned to you a moment ago what we advocated was that this should not be a Serb autonomous region, but that it should simply be the autonomous region of Birac. Afterwards, these political parties agreed to that and the decision was passed for it to be called the autonomous region of Birac. And there would be room there for all Serbs and Muslims in Yugoslavia or in -- within the boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. My question was more simple than that. I was asking you when you say what you believe was the reason for joining municipalities into these autonomous districts, you're speaking on behalf of or from your position in the SDP and not speaking on behalf of the intentions of the SDS members?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking -- well, the SDP and we -- we voted on behalf of the Serb people, and we wanted this kind of decision to be passed. We did not threaten the rights of the other people in any way by passing that decision, but what we advocated was that as far as the declaration on independence was concerned and also the referendum, we wanted to make sure in that region that we would enjoy all our rights on an equal footing with the other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So your interests and plans were aligned with those of the SDP -- I'm sorry, the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the decision that was made at the time was the decision that other peoples were involved as well. The decision was not only establishing an SAO, but only an autonomous region of Birac. Unfortunately, due to the events that were happening at a certain pace it was merely constituted but it never became operational due to the events that followed and which prevented the implementation of this decision in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm looking at the clock. I think this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us talk about more concrete issues after the break. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to paragraph 27 of your statement, in that paragraph you say: "The front lines in Vlasenica in April of 1992 were formed spontaneously when the Serbian and Muslim populations relocated on their own initiative and settled in villages where they were the majority." Now, there were military orders specifically related to moving Muslims out of this area, setting up prison camps and exchanging prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such orders. If we can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have P3240, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As that's coming up, this is an order from the 31st of May, 1992, from Major Svetozar Andric. And what you will see at the top of the document is it says: "Pursuant to the decision of the 'Birac' SAR, which regulates the moving out of the Muslim population from the territory of 'Birac' SAR, I hereby order ..." And then you have a list of four instructions: First, to set up a camp; second, not to arbitrarily liquidate the prisoners; third, to conduct interviews; and, fourth, to establish contact urgently regarding negotiations on the exchange of prisoners. Now, that does not sound like a spontaneous population movement, does it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have an opportunity to see this decision, but on the basis of the very fact that the commander Major Svetozar Andric is relying on is something that I'm not familiar with. I did not have an occasion to find out whether this decision of his was responded by any other organ in terms of adopting their own decisions. A while ago I said that the motives for setting up autonomous regions was -- however, here he speaks about SAR. I don't know what he meant by that and I don't know if the Prosecution has this decision that he is invoking for the Muslim population to be relocated. First of all, I know that this leadership was a self-proclaimed one, that due to the events it was unable to work, so unless I can see the original decision I cannot comment upon how this idea of moving out was designed and conceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's then move to something that you should be more familiar with, which relates to the actions of the municipal authorities where you say in statement paragraph 24 that the authorities had already formed commissions that went around the town and sealed the houses and flats of Muslims who had left Vlasenica so that their property would not be stolen. Now, my question to you is: Even though Muslim houses were sealed, they were later unsealed and assigned to Serbs by this commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Look, in that period --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon me for interrupting --

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: -- there was chaos --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon me for interrupting, Mr. Celikovic, but I think this is a very simple question. Isn't it true that they were later unsealed and assigned to Serbs by this commission?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that there was an invasion of Serbs who were expelled from Tuzla, Kladanj, Zivinice, the Serbian Gorazde, and other places in that period. There were nearly 2.500 refugees in Vlasenica at the time and accommodation was provided initially in a TO facility pending some permanent solution. There were no other possibilities to arrange that. They even spent some time in a hall in a school and also in a hotel. Later on the commission which was composed of members of the local authorities drew up records based on which they allocated this property for temporary use by the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in addition to allocating that property, there was some Serbs who forcibly broke into Muslim houses that had been left empty and some Serbs who forcibly evicted Muslim families from their houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: -- there were such cases not on a large scale but there were families who had abandoned their property or their property was torched and they even suffered casualties. So, quite simply, they were impatient and they couldn't wait for a property to be allocated to them through legal channels. So it did happen that they broke into houses, and very rarely some of them even maltreated certain Muslim families, threw them out, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, this happened [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: After that the municipal authorities tried to put this situation right in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This happened on a large enough scale that you say to prevent such cases from taking place again, this is in paragraph 26 of your statement, you say: "To spare the Muslim population from experiencing stress and mistreatment the municipal authority decided to turn the TO facilities into a reception centre where the remaining Muslims who had not left the municipality of Vlasenica could be housed in order to protect them from mistreatment or possible physical attacks." Now, just to make sure that I've understood you correctly, you're saying that because the Serbs were breaking into Muslim homes and evicting them from their own property, the municipal government's response was to set up a place for Muslims to go so they could abandon their property first; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just said that that was a situation bordering on chaos. There was a large number of refugees and, quite simply, the incumbent authorities or the public security station were able enough to provide protection to the population. Since the leadership -- the Muslim leadership had abandoned Vlasenica, individuals representing certain groups demanded on account of fear for their safety to be given temporary accommodation where they would enjoy better safety and security guarantees. And for that reason the authorities decided to offer this facility that had originally been used by the Serbs to the Muslims to be used. They also asked to be provided means of transport so that they can travel to Muslim-controlled areas until appropriate conditions were created and they were hence temporarily accommodated in a TO facility in Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you just said that the reason to send Muslims to Susica was to give them better safety and security guarantees. Now, this Trial Chamber has heard evidence that at that location approximately 500 to 550 people were held in a 15 by 30 metre concrete hangar, that they had to share ten unwashed plates when they were fed once a day, that they had to share a 10-litre pot to go to the bathroom in the evening hours and that when it was full they had to relieve themselves in their own clothes and that people were beaten to death among other things. For that I would cite Prosecution Exhibit 3212, page 31 to 35. Now, you would agree that does not sound like protecting people from mistreatment, does it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly it doesn't sound like that, but I am not sure that there is evidence that that was exactly the situation there. The fact is that the conditions were not fully proper but it was a temporary solution until such conditions were created for them to go to a desired location of their own choice in the areas where they wanted to go, be it Kladanj, Tuzla, Cerska, or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, you say that you doubt that there is evidence that that was exactly the situation there, but you never visited the Susica camp when it was being used to hold Muslims, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for logistics and as far as I remember, following a battalion commander's order I participated in making certain assessments before this facility was converted for other purposes. In that period, after the 4th Infantry Battalion was formed as part of the Sekovici Brigade, the command post of the logistic base of the battalion was relocated to Donja Zelkova [phoen], where I spent a certain period of time between June and October. Therefore, occasionally for the purpose of co-ordination, we had to go to Vlasenica, but I was not familiar with any details relating to the conditions and events taking place in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You say in your statement: "I do not know until when the Muslims remained in that building and what went on there." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I just told you. The command post was in Donja Zelkovi [phoen], it was some 10 kilometres from Vlasenica, and due to that I was absent from the location. Also, according to establishment, it was not my duty to handle any co-ordinating activities regarding this facility. Although, I must say, that within that facility or in one of the facilities, there was a quartermaster warehouse that was used by the 4th Infantry Battalion and which was independent of the other facilities. And this storehouse had its own guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. File. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very few, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celikovic, did you take part in the elections in 1996?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was any clearance needed to be provided by the OSCE in the international community for every individual regarding their time of war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive that clearance?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stood in the elections as a candidate on the Serbian Democratic Party list and that period we shared power with the Serbian Radical Party who had won the elections and who appointed the president during that period, and I was the president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that the voters did not believe that the Serbian Democratic Party was not radical enough and that therefore they voted for the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I have to object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. How do you explain that the Radicals had won the elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the Serbian party is also accused here or branded as an extreme organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no -- just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that ordinary people were even more extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That wasn't the thrust of the questions that were put on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked with regard to P3240 document - and I kindly ask this document to be shown - you were asked whether you were able to distinguish between detainees and prisoners -- actually, I'm asking that question of you, Mr. Celikovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Detainees were individuals who were in possession of illegal weapons, but after certain checks had been made it was confirmed that they, indeed, held illegal weapons, as a result of which the public security station filed a large number of criminal reports. And they were kept there until exchanges were conducted in the collection centre in Batkovici where they were later moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to explain to me the term "prisoner." How does one become a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, prisoners were individuals who, for example, let's be specific -- there was a group of 150 or so prisoners deployed on the combat line facing Memici and they were captured. Those were able-bodied men and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can we please ask for item 2 to be properly translated because it relates to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celikovic, Mr. File asked you - and it was implied in his question - that these houses were given to the Serbs. Was there ever a single instance when ownership was changed; i.e., that by an illegal decision on the part of the authorities property was confiscated for someone and given to someone else?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those were merely temporary solutions for temporary use. Later, when the conditions were ripe, all these properties were reinstated to those who had originally used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more question. What was the attitude of the authorities towards individuals who took the solution of their housing problems into their own hands and harassed the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the authorities at the time, especially, for example, the public security station where certain individuals took it into own hands to file criminal reports and to solve those issues within the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question. The international representative in the period between 1997, 1998, or even up to 2000, how many legally elected Serb representatives were removed from their office?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of the exact number, but I do know that certain officials were subject to sanctions. I told you that I myself in 1999 and in 2004 - and I know that in 2004 over 60 officials mainly from the SDS were under sanctions. And I think that a total number is more than 200. So six or seven years later they were rehabilitated, as it were, although I don't understand this notion quite well because their sanctions were removed. But these people were left jobless, their families were broken, and, quite simply, their livelihood was jeopardised. It was not only a matter of them not being able to participate in elections, but their whole existence was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of them instituted lawsuits against the government?

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that a small number of them, maybe just individual cases, were of that nature. But I do believe and I want to hope that once we have the rule of law these cases will be dealt with because every government has a duty of care to protect its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: SAVO CELIKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Celikovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on behalf of the Chamber I'd like to thank you. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we take a very short break between witnesses just for relocation purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure five minutes is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.31 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In English or this language? [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you don't mind before starting your question, I'm not Jepinic, I'm Zepinic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E) --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say incriminate I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer would incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand very well what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zepinic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Good day, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please bear the following in mind - I'd also like to remind yourself as well - that we pause between my questions and your answers and also let us speak at a slower pace because I really want the transcript to reflect accurately everything we are saying. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I gave a statement to Mr. Robinson when he visited me in London last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D05659 in e-court. 1D05659.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you have the statement in front of you, do you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read that statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I received it by e-mail, a copy that I checked, and then I signed it and returned it to Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page so that we can identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I certify that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I reviewed this statement and it does generally reflect what we discussed when Mr. Robinson came to visit me in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers basically be the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to envisage that I will be able to paraphrase each and every word, but at any rate I shall respond to every one of your questions and all the questions of the other party and I will say what I said in this statement and what I confirmed by my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to put questions to you now, but if I were to put the same questions that were put to you by my Defence team would your answers to the same questions be basically the same as they are in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the statement that I gave and signed is something that I am not willing to change in any way so that I would say something different, even if I were to be subjected to any kind of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In addition to this document there are seven associated exhibits that we're seeking to tender, all of which are actually on our 65 ter list this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Among them with respect to 65 ter number 31878, which is referred to in paragraph 44, I think the -- there's some mistake in terms of 65 ter number because that intercept seems to be related to 27th of August, 1991, which is different from the date referred to in the paragraph. So with the exception -- that exception, do you have any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President, other than to note that 65 ter 31878 is P02963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Which I just referred to; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And 65 ter 30234 is P05869, at least that's what our records show.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] some objection. I'm not quite sure in the summary given to here on the page 2, last paragraph, I don't think that was Ismet Delalic Celo, I think it was Ramiz Delalic, Celo, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic should have noted it. Yes, then we'll admit those six associated exhibits. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
