utterances.text: Yes, you're exactly correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we give the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we give the number for the Rule 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's Exhibit D2923.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the other six items in -- will be given numbers in due course liaising amongst the court deputy and the parties. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read out the summary of Dr. Zepinic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the summary is not evidence. It is information. But thank you for this correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Vitomir Zepinic was deputy minister of interior for Bosnia and Herzegovina from January the 30th, 1991, to April the 4th, 1992. After the 1990 elections, Dr. Zepinic was invited to attend a meeting with the SDS leadership, including Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and others. They told him that pursuant to an agreement among the national parties which had won the elections, the SDS was able to designate the deputy minister of interior. During his meeting, Dr. Zepinic made his position quite clear. He was not a member of the SDS or any other party and not voted -- had not voted on the 1990 elections, and would not become an SDS party member. He was committed to a professional and a non-political Ministry of Interior with the most qualified people regardless -- with the most qualified people regardless of their ethnicity. He was a proponent of the continuation of a multi-cultural society in Bosnia. Dr. Karadzic defended Dr. Zepinic against other members of the SDS who argued that the post should go to a loyal SDS party member. Dr. Karadzic stated that he wanted a competent professional in the job and that it would make it more difficult for the other parties to criticise SDS if the person they nominated was of high calibre, professional, and known to be independent. During his time as a deputy minister of interior, Dr. Zepinic was regularly confronted with problems in allocating posts within the Ministry of Interior. Overall, Dr. Zepinic had more problems with the President Izetbegovic and Ejub Ganic than he did with Dr. Karadzic regarding these issues. They were more extreme, were surrounded by a cadre of the extreme nationalists, and more often tried to use their power to manipulate the appointment of personnel within the Ministry of Interior. Dr. Zepinic believes that President Izetbegovic is most responsible for the outbreak of war in Bosnia, considering his role as president of BH -- of the BH Presidency. Like with other political leaders, Dr. Zepinic had quite frequent conversations with Dr. Karadzic, at meetings and on the telephone. Most of the conversations pertained to personnel discussions within the Ministry of the Interior or events which threatened the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. During his contacts with Dr. Karadzic while he was deputy minister of interior, Dr. Zepinic never understood him to desire the expulsion of Muslims or Croats. From his knowledge of Dr. Karadzic's personality, he does not believe that Dr. Karadzic would have favoured this and he knows that Dr. Karadzic had close friends in Sarajevo who were Muslims and Croats. As deputy minister of interior, Dr. Zepinic had access to a great deal of information collected by ministry operatives on the policy of the national parties, as expressed at Assembly meetings, Executive Committee meetings, and the official party documents. He was not aware that it was the SDS party policy to favour the expulsions of members of other ethnic groups. Dr. Karadzic often expressed the view that Serbs could not live together with the Muslims. Dr. Zepinic understood this to mean that they could not live together politically or culturally, not physically. He never understood Dr. Karadzic to favour physical separation of the Serbs and other ethnic groups through expulsions. On 1st of March, 1992, a Serb was murdered by Ramiz Delalic, Celo, a Muslim at wedding ceremony in a church in Sarajevo. The Ministry of Interior arrested Delalic and Delalic told the crime inspectors that the killing had been ordered by President Izetbegovic. Based upon all of the information the Ministry of Interior had at the time, Dr. Zepinic believed that Delalic was telling the truth. This was confirmed when he was released with no charges -- when Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was released with no charges against him were filed. Dr. Zepinic believed that President Izetbegovic wanted to provoke a conflict with the Serbs. The Serbs reacted by erecting the barricades in Sarajevo. Dr. Zepinic worked hard to negotiate an end to this crisis, travelling to the barricades during the night. He called upon President Izetbegovic for help, but he declined, saying that this was a police matter. Ejub Ganic who was in charge of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency was also completely uninterested in helping to solve this problem. Dr. Zepinic was very familiar with the events in Bijeljina on 1st and 2nd of April, 1992, and was involved in trying to end the violence there. He was privy of reports and intelligence informations about the events in Bijeljina on those days. Dr. Zepinic was convinced that Dr. Radovan Karadzic had nothing to do with the killings in Bijeljina on the 1st and 2nd of April, 1992. Those killings were perpetrated by Arkan and his men, who came to Bijeljina to loot. Based upon all the sources of information Dr. Zepinic had about the event, he did not believe that Dr. Karadzic had anything to do with Arkan's coming to Bijeljina or Arkan's criminal activities when he arrived there. When the war broke out, Dr. Zepinic chose to remain at the apartment -- at his apartment in Sarajevo. He was arrested on several occasions by the Muslim paramilitary forces. He finally managed to leave Sarajevo and arrived in Belgrade around July the 19th, 1992. In late August 1992, he was arrested by Mico Stanisic and others in Belgrade and taken to Republika Srpska. He was detained until the end of November, when he was driven to Belgrade on the understanding that he would see his family and return to Republika Srpska. Dr. Zepinic did not return, but instead immigrated to Australia in February 1993. And that would be the summary. For the moment I don't have other questions for Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And it's one minute past noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have just experienced an efficient form of bringing your evidence before the Court, and I will attempt to be equally efficient and not squander the information you have previously provided to this Tribunal either in the form of testimony or statements in the past. And just to remind you, as I'm sure you're aware, you have provided information on numerous occasions, including a statement over the course of four days in 2002, a statement to Canadian authorities in 2006, during which you essentially confirmed the accuracy of your 2002 statement, a statement in 2008, testimony before the Stanisic and Zupljanin Trial Chamber in 2010. And I will be focusing on the information that you provided on those previous occasions, trying to, as much as possible, ask questions in a manner that can simply be answered yes or no. I notice that you made the observation that -- about paraphrasing the previous statement you gave in the context of Dr. Karadzic's questions about the statement that was just admitted into evidence. I won't be asking you to paraphrase your previous evidence because when we take time for that purpose it keeps us from moving on to the next bit of information you've previously provided. So with all that in mind - and I apologise for that lengthy introduction - I'll move forward to ask the questions I have. First of all, Dr. Zepinic, as you indicated in your 2002 statement and again in your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, you were against the ethnic division of the police. And as you said in 2002: "If we were going to accept that police were established on a national basis, then there was no safe place in Bosnia." Is that correct? And that's found at English page 6 of the 2002 statement.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. Do I need to answer you in English or in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I answer your question, I have an objection to this summary presented by Dr. Karadzic. On page 1 I always claimed and I wish to reiterate it in the courtroom here, it wasn't that the national parties were elected in the elections of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were set up as a coalition and this was supported by the European Union, the elections that were held in November 1990 had a vote of 41.4 of the entire electorate. So there wasn't even a simple majority let alone a two-thirds majority, and that was compulsory on the basis of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to have a valid outcome. 43.6 is the vote that was received by Fikret Abdic who had the largest number of votes, followed by Izetbegovic. And that is to say that not a single one of these members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had received the mandate of the people as an elected member of parliament or the Presidency. Mr. Tieger, in terms of your question, I remained committed to the principle that this is a powder keg to have this division along ethnic lines and I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to amplify that a bit, as you testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case and I think the reference to powder keg makes that sufficiently clear, you believed that the splitting of the MUP would result in an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We had information about paramilitary formations of all three parties and also armed elements of national parties as well as certain paramilitary formations that had come either from Croatia or from Serbia, and we regularly reported to the Presidency about that. If you allow me, I am going to read the conclusions of the session of the Presidency that was held --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the basis of the information provided by the State Security Service, we had the exact number of members of sabotage groups that were infiltrated from Croatia and the number of paramilitary units that were formed by national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the ministry were to be split up, then this would inevitably lead to an armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Zepinic or Dr. Zepinic, excuse me. You --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note -- first of all, I notice you have certain documents in front of you. If you --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- have occasion to feel the need to refer to those documents, I would simply ask that you ask for leave from the Court, indicate what you want to look at so everyone in the courtroom is aware of what information is being referred to. Secondly, to the extent possible, I would ask you to wait for some kind of invitation to elaborate on a question before you do so. I'm well aware of the fact that you have a great deal of information about events at that time. I'm attempting to get as much of the information that I believe is relevant at this point to the Court, and I have a limited time to do that. So every time you expand on a particular point, it prevents me from -- it may prevent me from asking questions about points later on. So I'm not trying to hamstring you unfairly, but to the extent possible if you can be guided by the question and wait for an invitation from either the Bench or myself or Dr. Karadzic to elaborate more fully on a question that's asked. Thank you. You referred in paragraph 13 of your statement to Boro and Ramiz --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement with you, Dr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you explain that Boro and Ramiz were a symbol of unity between persons of different nationality. And is it correct that they were a symbol generally of the concept of brotherhood and unity that in former Yugoslavia was the fundamental principle for 50 years? And I believe you said that in your 2008 statement, refer to the fact that brotherhood and unity had been the fundamental principle in former Yugoslavia for 50 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can I give my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Well, you see Boro and Ramiz were two symbols. These were indeed historical persons from the Second World War. Their ethnic backgrounds were different. But how do I put this? They represented the brotherhood and unity that was there when opposing the occupiers during the Second World War. Now, why were Delimustafic and I proclaimed Boro and Ramiz? Well, I don't know. You know, journalist dealt with this very skillfully in the press and there were pictures there as well. So there was in model of unity in the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior, and this probably led to this declaration of Boro and Ramiz by the president, by the public in general. Now, whether I'm Boro or Ramiz, I cannot give you an answer to that. And after all, it doesn't matter. But my initiative and my leadership in the Ministry of the Interior advocated what had been a principle for 50 years in the previous Yugoslavia; that is brotherhood and unity and respect for all the differences, cultural, religious, et cetera, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. This concept was carried through to the extent possible within the Ministry of the Interior itself to the best of my ability. However, Mr. Tieger, just as my unfortunate former country felt, well, everybody loved it and appreciated it and yet it went down the drain and then everybody loved and appreciated us and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have previously stated - and you did so in your 2008 statement at page 7, paragraph 36 - that for Radovan Karadzic this concept of brotherhood and unity that you explained did not exist; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: The concept of how national parties operated, including the SDS, the concept of brotherhood and unity was not known to have been promoted throughout the whole mandate that they acquired. Let me remind you, Mr. Tieger, in their election memorandum or platform - and I can quote Dr. Karadzic, saying that the function and the role and the task of national parties was to preserve brotherhood and unity in Yugoslavia was a historical legacy of President Tito and that they should preserve it as their best treasure. If possible, I can give you exactly the name of the document where this statement can be found, but let me tell you that the national parties went astray quite a lot and started dealing only with national matters and they neglected the concept of unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was only quoting from the 2008 statement, but let me be somewhat more specific about the explanations you've provided about Dr. Karadzic's view of this issue. You stated also in your 2008 statement, and that's found at page 4 of the English: "It was the belief of Karadzic that different ethnicities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, BiH, could not live together. He never gave a reasonable explanation or provided any evidence of why he maintained these views. This concept also became the or was the general policy of the SDS." And I said it's page 4 -- that's at page 7 of the B/C/S. That's correct, that's what you -- that's the information you provided to the OTP in 2008; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, not only as far as the party is concerned and its programme. Any political party. But that was a reflection of how the National Assembly operated. Only the interests, national interests, of deputies came to the fore during sessions. There was never any room for the principled views and attitudes of ordinary citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that was something that was maintained and consistently implemented both at their political rallies but also on the sessions of the government and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your testimony during the Stanisic/Zupljanin case you explained further that you had many conversations with Dr. Karadzic, and this is found at transcript page 5705 in e-court page 27. "Regarding his view that, you know, life together between two nationalities in -- in former Yugoslavia or Bosnia, pardon me, is impossible." And that's correct also, isn't it, Dr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: In view of the concept and the policies pursued by national parties, it was obvious that two nationalist parties cannot live together and they cannot attain a joint objective together in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's nothing new. In my private talks with Dr. Karadzic we discussed this matter and I was not convinced that he really thought about physically elimination of non-Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the fact remains that the extremism of nationalist parties created a climate in which it was impossible to achieve coexistence, as Dr. Tudjman used to say, and to reconcile this concept with the policies pursued by nationalist parties. If you allow me, that is why Dr. Tudjman proposed Bosnia-Herzegovina to be divided between Serbia and Croatia and you know that these meetings did happen and President Mesic spoke extensively about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during those talks with Dr. Karadzic and -- he said that life together between -- in Bosnia between two nationalities is impossible, you responded to his comments about that issue by pointing out to him that your sister was married to a Muslim and as you said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case: "I asked him if Serbs and Muslims cannot live together can you tell me on which was -- I will say to my sister that her husband is not a good guy ..." and so on. In short, when Dr. Karadzic explained his view of the nationalities being unable to live together, you said: What happens to my family? What happens to my brother-in-law; correct? That's found at the Stanisic/Zupljanin case transcript page 5706.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not only about what was going to happen with my family but what will happen with about 65 per cent of mixed families in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was not only the issue that I had a relative in a mixed marriage because I originate from a place that was proportionally speaking the most dominant Serb municipality in the former Yugoslavia. But let me remind you that the SDS did not win the election in Sekovici of which Dr. Karadzic accused me on many occasions and laid blame on me for that. So as I said, it was not only my personal family problem. The problem was the whole population of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had an enormous percentage of ethnically mixed marriages. How can you physically divide or separate a high-rise building or flats on the same floor? How can one expect that such a division would be a guarantee of peaceful life among neighbours. Such policy pursued by the nationalist party was something that I was really not able to swallow, if you allow me to say that, and I don't believe that Dr. Karadzic was able either. I think that he faced problems among his own ranks from his own extremists, and you heard here evidence that there were people who advocated the expulsion of everyone who was against the Serb policy, including Dr. Zepinic, not because I was on the front and because I fought SDS. I was arrested because I disagreed with the concept of the SDA concept as well as that of the SDS. That's a fact that, Mr. Tieger, I explain to you that I share the destiny of my former country. Everybody used to love and appreciate me, but nobody wanted me. That's it. What can one do about it? [In English] Does that satisfy your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There will be more questions along this line, Dr. Zepinic. In addition to the conversations --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that you had with Dr. Karadzic about this issue, you were also aware that Mrs. Plavsic maintained that Serbs and other nationalities could not live together, which prompted you to say to her that an attempt to separate the ethnic communities would produce violence and thousands of innocent civilians would be killed. And that's found at -- in your 2002 statement at page 5: "I informed her that if you tried to separate the ethnic communities, then there would be violence and thousands of innocent civilians would be killed." That's a correct reflection of what's in your statement and the information you provided?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by that statement. Unfortunately, I was overly optimistic because the events that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina were much more tragic than I had anticipated. So that is my answer that I gave often to Biljana Plavsic and Koljevic at our meetings. And I knew that Dr. Karadzic personally had problems with those two because, quite simply, they always said that the attitude that I subscribed to was an unacceptable one and that the party should do something about it. As you know, I offered my resignation twice to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister. My resignation was rejected. On the 13th of May [as interpreted]I told the prime minister and the president of the Assembly and the presiding member of the Presidency that I was not going to resign, but that I expected them to have the guts to force my resignation. They didn't have that power and that is how this thing was resolved. So let me say that members of the Presidency, instead of being a collective organ heading the state, were more nationalistic than nationalist leaders themselves, including Mate Boban and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence - the interpreters didn't catch - you after "Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the Presidency, instead of taking a joint position as the head of state, they were more concerned about nationalist interests, including the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, who violated the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina by holding at the same time the post of the president of the party and the president of the Presidency. Quite often he acted at the Presidency meetings as the leader of the SDA instead of as the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Dr. Koljevic in an earlier -- well, first of all, you said your -- let me clarify something quickly. You said your resignation was rejected on the 13th of May. You told the prime minister and the president of the Assembly and the presiding member of the Presidency that you were not going to resign. Did you mean that date or did you mean another date. It was translated as "May 13th."

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Sometime in early March 1991, when I realised how the situation was progressing I decided that I cannot accept the concept of these parties and I offered my resignation to the persons mentioned before, who rejected it because they believed that that would be a risky move for the further developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mentioned the 13th of May because the 13th of May was the date of security forces, but nobody from the authorities found any decency to send a celebratory card to the security services for their day. I was the person who acted professionally in every respect and in every situation and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: -- the reason why I managed to survive. [In English] Please. Please. [Interpretation] I sent a telegram and I congratulated the holiday to all members of the security forces, but I didn't include members from the authorities because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you slow down a bit. The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start again from where you said you sent a telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the exception of Mr. Krajisnik and at my insistence, he was the only one who sent his congratulations. I insisted that others should do the same. I didn't expect them to organise any ceremonies to give them any medals, et cetera. But I said that they cannot expect any congratulations coming from people in the authorities who were criminals. I don't know who organised this rally. I was invited to attend it. Mr. Krajisnik was there, Joran Livan [phoen] was there, Nikola Koljevic was there. I said that I stood by the telegram that I had sent, that I could simply -- could not comprehend why they resent what I wrote in it. I would like them to request my resignation and that I myself was not going to resign on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 10 Dr. Zepinic said that it was not possible to expect congratulations from people that the service used to deal beforehand including Mr. Izetbegovic was not in the transcript as well as what he said that Mr. Izetbegovic was really rude at that meeting. I would like to ask the witness to speak more slowly because we are really dealing here with the shades of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, please, just one moment. We're about to adjourn because of the time. I certainly am trying to respect your desire to get as much information as you consider useful to the Court, before the Court, as possible. And I ask for the same respect in return. I will be moving on to various topics. I gave you an opportunity to clarify the date. That was not meant to be an invitation for an elaboration of the circumstances surrounding that resignation letter in March 1991. And there will be many topics that are important to the Court that I won't be able to cover if you don't allow me to guide you to the particular subject areas. So I would appreciate that very much. Unfortunately we're at the break now and we'll be able to resume after the lunch recess.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Chamber like to hear whether the witness confirmed my intervention and what was omitted originally in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I stated the same twice so it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it doesn't seem to have made its way to the transcript, but do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. This was not recorded because I spoke too fast and after that you warned me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would request to you to slow down when we resume after 45-minutes' break. So we'll take a break and resume at 18 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, when you were explaining to the Court what you said in -- to Mrs. Plavsic in response to her comments that Serbs and other nationalities could not live together, you also mentioned that that was an answer you gave often to Biljana Plavsic and Koljevic. So just to round that out it is correct, isn't it, as you stated in your 2002 statement at page 6 that Nikola Koljevic also said that the ethnic communities could not live together and, in fact, stated that the Serbs should just expel the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to make a comment. I believe that of members of the Presidency, particularly Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, I think that Koljevic was really extreme in his nationalistic attitudes. His statement that it was impossible for the Serbs to live with anyone else was something that he repeatedly mentioned in various situations as a slogan. And due to that, we were often at loggerheads on many occasions. I even talked to the prime minister, seeking possible intervention from their part to put a stop to this, although we were talking about a member of the Presidency, but in his actions and in his views deviated from what was decided in March, was that any party advocating the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina along ethnic lines cannot be registered. So I agree with you, this is not something that he said once or twice. That is something that he commonly said. He underlined that and these extreme views of his became very evident at some of the most important meetings and gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to a somewhat different topic. As you stated in your 2008 statement, the national parties wanted candidates for the MUP who were loyal to or favoured the party that nominated them, so interference was always present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes. All three parties tried in every possible way to create a situation to have officials, particularly in executive positions, who were loyal to their political party, regardless of their qualification or competence, and that based on an inter parte agreement a parity was established between ethnic communities and their representation in the MUP, and therefore the parties were the ones who nominated the candidates. Unfortunately in the majority of cases I rejected those candidates because they had no idea whatsoever about what they were supposed to do in the ministry, never mind if they were on excellent terms from -- with another official in the MUP or with someone from their party. Very often we in the ministry had arguments and rows with the political parties over their nominations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And specifically, as you stated in your 2008 statement at page 4: "Karadzic telephoned me on many occasions and discussed some particular candidates. He always wanted to have some influence on the appointments. Alija Izetbegovic as well as Stjepan Kljujic sometimes tried to interfere but not as much as Karadzic." Correct? That's what you stated in 2008 and that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct -- [In English] Sorry, I apologise to you. [Interpretation] It is correct that Karadzic called me more often about Serb candidates than Izetbegovic and Kljujic did that regarding their candidates because they often bypassed me. In most cases they would agree that with Delimustafic or Kvesic or somebody else who was my assistant and after that I would have to examine who the candidates were and then I had to go back to Kljujic and intervene, although I relied more on Mate Boban because Kljujic was so incompetent that I didn't want to have any dealings with him. So I contacted most often with Mate Boban regarding Croatian candidates and it was Omer Behmeh with regards to Muslim candidates, except when an intervention came from Mr. Izetbegovic. So generally speaking, Dr. Karadzic called me more often than the other two because, as I said, they tried to circumvent me because they were aware that I would not accept their proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were, as you stated in 2008, opposed generally to SDS policy; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was against any nationalistic policy in the country, not only the one pursued by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous answer Dr. Zepinic said that if they -- if he saw who the candidates were, he would explode. That means that he would be so enraged and none of that was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I lost track -- what line did you refer to, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 10 [In English] No, no, when "Kljujic and intervene, although I relied more on Mate Boban because Kljujic was incompetent ... so I contacted most often Mate Boban." And it is here line 10 "Croatian candidates and it was Omer Behmeh with regards to Muslim candidates" [Interpretation] And in this portion Dr. Zepinic says: When I saw who the candidates were, I would explode and I would then appeal to Mr. Izetbegovic to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've just confirmed a moment ago you were opposed generally to SDS policy. It's correct that others in the MUP were not opposed to or in conflict with SDS policy. For example, as you stated in your 2008 statement: "Mico Stanisic," or Stanic I think it says there, "tried as much as he could to please Karadzic instead of doing his job." And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct and that's why he was replaced. [In English] I dismissed him from his position because of him looking more about policy proclaimed by Dr. Karadzic than Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now at paragraphs 32 through 52 of your statement you discuss some telephone conversations in which Dr. Karadzic referred to various events and raised the prospect of the division of the MUP or the country. It is correct that since the time of those discussions you have become aware of various events or meetings which you did not attend at which the division of the MUP was concretely discussed by Bosnian Serb officials. For example, you testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case about the 11 February 1992 meeting in Banja Luka which you did not attend and did not know about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, that meeting is reflected in P1083 and contains various references to the decision to establish Serbian MUP. And it is also correct, Dr. Zepinic, that you didn't attend Assembly meetings -- an Assembly meeting in late March 1992 when Dr. Karadzic talked about the establishment of the Republika Srpska MUP, which he indicated could happen in two or three days; and noted that at that moment Serbian municipalities would "literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned." That's correct, you -- is it correct you were not aware of that or did not attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I attended only meetings of the Assemblies of national parties when it was the Ministry of Interior that was discussed. And when I was invited to come I did not attend most of them, or rather, I did not attend most of the Assemblies so I do not remember this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand from your 2008 statement that you were told about an Assembly session in late March 1992 by Stojan Zupljanin and he mentioned that and told you that there was an initiative to split the MUP. That's a 2008 statement page 13; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Actually, I found out about this idea of separating the MUP into the three ethnic communities. This proposal was first presented at the meeting with Mr. Cutileiro in January 1992. I was terribly surprised when I saw that members of the government attended that meeting, Mr. Djeric and Mr. Mahmut Cehajic, and then at the next government meeting I raised that question. I asked in which capacity they attended that meeting and in which capacity was it for them to tacitly approve of that proposal and on the other hand the minister and the deputy minister of the interior had no idea about that. I put that question to Mr. Izetbegovic and then I was accused of spying on members of the Presidency and the delegation that had this meeting with Mr. Cutileiro. So if I was spying them, then yes, I was, because it was my duty to find out what it was they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, as I believe you made clear in your 2008 statement at page 11, you felt sufficiently strongly about splitting the MUP along ethnic lines that you would have arrested Dr. Karadzic and the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership when that happened and the reason you didn't is that you would have been shot; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry for -- [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether they would have shot me. You have to ask them about that. At any rate, I did not decide to arrest the national leaders, or rather, the members of the Presidency. I wasn't really interested in power, to be frank. Through my ministry and through the role that I played, I tried to ensure that the state functioned. I didn't want to cause a crisis. 20 years later, my friend [In English] It's probably quite difficult to understand what happened 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, I was simply quoting from the 2008 statement where you explained you wanted to clarify that you took no action on --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, because -- at least you felt you would have been shot?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to speak to you now about the meeting referred to at paragraphs 67 through 70 of your statement at which you tendered your resignation. And, first of all, that meeting was on the 4th of April, which would have been just a few days after the dispatch sent by Momcilo Mandic; correct? And you nodded your head?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you met with Mandic and Stanisic after that dispatch, as you explained in your 2002 statement at page 10, and told them that you did not recognise the decisions of either Radovan Karadzic or Momcilo Krajisnik and did not recognise the decisions of any parliament constituted on one national basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. All members of the collegium attended the meeting. It wasn't only Mandic and Stanisic. And the other details you referred to are quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then on the 4th of April you met with members of the SDS leadership - that's how they're described in paragraph 68 of the statement - and that included Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Professor Buha, Momcilo Mandic, and Mico Stanisic; correct? That's what you said in your 2002 statement.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Stanisic said at that meeting, again according to the 2002 statement as you've explained it, that you were destroying their concept. And when you asked: What concept? They said the concept to divide the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you told them that if they did something like this, that is, split the MUP, then "they would be responsible for the forthcoming conflict because it was impossible to do this peacefully." That's at 2002 statement, pages 12 to 13; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. But may I just explain this to you a bit. As a matter of fact, I expressed my admiration at the fact that they were prepared to take over this role of waging war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the entire catastrophe that would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic explained that the SDS had strong support from Belgrade and that they had strong support from the JNA and the army would be on their side; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That was his explanation although I did not believe that because my co-operation with the JNA was much better than that of the Serb Democratic Party. You can take a look at the record of the meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 15th of October with General Kadijevic and his coworkers, where full support was expressed. How do I put this? Also, they paid tribute to the co-operation that the MUP and the JNA had in establishing check-points in Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to prevent incursions by paramilitary groups and criminal groups involved in money laundering, smuggling, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to that expression of strong support -- expression by Dr. Karadzic about strong support from the JNA and the army being on his side, it's correct as you explained to the Canadian authorities, isn't it, that you and Dr. Karadzic -- that your understanding, as you discussed with Dr. Karadzic many times, was that he always mentioned that the JNA will be on his side; right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's what he said, but my meetings with General Kadijevic and General Vasiljevic, General Kukanjac, Uzelac, and other officers of the JNA did not give me that feeling. That was not expressed to such an extent as presented by Dr. Karadzic in terms of the support that he would receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Zepinic, back to the meeting at which your resignation was offered on April 4th. As you explained in the Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic were "extremely aggressive" about your opposition to the concept of ethnically based parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that Dr. Karadzic was aggressive. If I may confirm, Karadzic and Krajisnik, to a degree tried to pacify the situation, but Koljevic was rather aggressive and then we squabbled and then he turned to Dr. Karadzic and said, "Well, look at what he's doing to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The quote is -- and I'm certainly happy to have you see it if you wish, but the parties can follow with me as I read it. That's on transcript page 5828 and the quote I was referring to is at line 15: "Dr. Karadzic and especially the late Dr. Koljevic were extremely aggressive with regard to my opposition of the concept of ethnically based parties."

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you explained in your 2002 statement they began to accuse and threaten you when you continued to refuse to join them and Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic said you were an idiot and that "it was impossible for the nationalities to live together." And that's found at the 2002 statement at page 14.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I admit that I am an idiot because I hadn't eliminated them before that meeting. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mico Stanisic produced a gun to shoot you saying: "We can't come to terms with this guy in other ways so let's kill him to prevent him causing any further headache." That's found in your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony at transcript page 5832.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But you know what? I don't think that, frankly speaking, Mico had the courage to shoot me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After about half an hour of threatening you, according to your 2002 statement, they let you leave and you went down to enter your car with your chauffeur, Zoran; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you enter the car your driver burst out in tears and said that he had been ordered by Mr. Mandic to kill you, otherwise they would kill his family. And he, your driver, who had been your driver for a long time said to you, "Minister, I cannot kill you." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. And, as you can see, he had not killed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, earlier in your testimony you made some reference to your arrest and imprisonment. That's found in particular at paragraphs 74 through 78 of your statement. And I want to ask you about the imprisonment which began in late August 1992. That's following your arrest by Mr. Stanisic in Belgrade. Now, you learned on the fifth or sixth day of your imprisonment, as you explained in your 2002 statement, that Dr. Karadzic was extremely aggressive toward you and had stated that you should be killed, but insisted that the investigation and procedure should be completed first because it had been publicly announced by Stanisic that you'd been arrested but then you should be killed. That's found at the 2002 statement, English pages 17; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You know, there were different attempts that were made to undermine me, to kill me physically. I have the original of the decision on my arrest. If you allow me I'm going to read it out now. Dr. Zepinic, doctor of medicine, residing in Sarajevo is hereby arrested on the basis of Article 119 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And then I'm given the right to appeal against that decision to the district court in Sarajevo and I'm in prison in Pale. So I'm in prison and this is the signature of Tomo Kovac on behalf of Mico Stanisic as minister of the interior. I was arrested on the basis of the Criminal Code of the SFRY by members of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in the territory of another state, Serbia, and as such I was taken to the prison in Pale. What I wish to say by this is that as far as arrests were concerned then there was a reference to federal laws and they abided by all federal laws, principles, constitutionality, and so on. However, when interests of the national party were at stake, then the federal laws were against the national party. What you said is correct. Now, whether there were agreements or not for me to be killed, I don't know, but I just do know that Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic, the minister of the interior of Serbia, intervened with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic asking to have me released from detention. I'm saying that because I had a telephone conversation with Mr. Bogdanovic and he told me during this conversation that the following was promised to him, that an investigation had to be made for about a few days and then together with my mentor, Professor Sternic, they were waiting for me. And then the next day Minister Bogdanovic called me and asked me why I wasn't in Belgrade, why I hadn't been released, and that they betrayed him, they betrayed Mr. Milosevic, and Professor Sternic was the connection involved because Mr. Milosevic's body-guard, personal body-guard, Senta was the connection because his wife worked as a nurse for Dr. Sternic. And then I was transferred to Kula near Lukavica, the prison there, and I spent some time there. That is where I gave that famous interview at the request of Dr. Karadzic, that was the explanation that was given to me. He was not quite pleased with what I said. But, Dr. Karadzic, I still stand by what I stated in that interview. After that I was transferred to the military prison at the Lukavica barracks, and then sometime late in November -- I really have to point out that Colonel Lugonja was very fair at the time. I was unable to go and visit my family and then in the meantime I was visited in the military prison twice by Dr. Karadzic. The first time he gave me an offer of having lunch at General Galic's office and I told him that I had already had lunch. And I asked where my family was and he knew that full well. And I -- or rather, he asked me whether I knew where my family was and I said that they were in a safe place because I knew why he was asking that. And then the second time we met just in passing. And since I was allowed to go and visit my family after having spent a few months in prison, I took advantage of the situation and I escaped. I do apologise to Zoran Kos, who was warden of the prison at the time and he acted as my driver and I said, "Just wait a minute. I want to see my family." I haven't seen him since and we hid in different places in Serbia until the end of January when we left Yugoslavia. I secured a visa and I left my country, or rather, I arrived in Australia on the 16th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Three relatively quick questions about that period of incarceration. First of all, you mentioned you knew why Dr. Karadzic was asking about your family. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My family was maltreated, especially my family -- especially my parents. My mother was killed in this maltreatment. Dr. Karadzic knows that full well. And I don't know why they touched my mother. Dr. Karadzic, in Orthodoxy an attack against one's mother is the greatest crime of all, and you know that very well. You and I had many discussions on many occasions and we talked about the love you had for your own mother and about your relationship with her. I'm sorry that that happened. My parents, my mother, are not to be blamed at all for my disagreement with national parties. My parents didn't agree with national parties either and I'm sorry that they ended the way they did because of me. I really would not like to go on on that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Doctor, but just to finish it and be clear: Did you understand the inquiry to be a form of pressure on you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that pressure from those who were carrying out the investigation. But I have to note that members of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska also regularly informed me about everything that was being agreed upon within the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party that had to do with me. If I can put it this way, I still had authority and a reputation among the members of the Ministry of the Interior. Dr. Karadzic knows that full well. You know, it was very important. Mr. Izetbegovic did the same thing too. I mean, let's be clear on that. At the time when I was in -- under house arrest in Sarajevo and when I was often brought in for different interviews. So I was informed by my former members of the police of what they were preparing for me while I was in prison in Pale and in Lukavica. And - how do I put this? - I know that there was this pressure that was brought to bear in terms of finding out where my wife and my children were. However, my old parents did not move from the place where they had been staying. So for nights and nights - I'm saying "nights" - because usually two or three idiots would come in and maltreat my parents from 10.00 p.m. until 4.00 a.m. and that was being repeated time and again. I didn't feel sorry about the fact that they could have killed me. Well, that was their decision. They are in power, they have weapons, I don't. I could understand that. To this day I can understand that because either one side or the other side or the third side may make an attempt to liquidate me physically, and there were such attempts because of disagreement. However, I can never understand nor can I ever accept that on account of that my mother had to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two more --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please. Transcript, please. In line 21 Dr. Zepinic said: Dr. Karadzic asked me to join him, and that sentence is not included in the transcript. So line 21: Dr. Karadzic knows that full well. Dr. Karadzic [In English] asks me to join. [Interpretation] Is that what you said? Ask me to join. And then it says, you know, it was very important, Izetbegovic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, two more hopefully quick follow-up questions about Kula. While you were interned in Kula in September and October, is it correct, as you explained in your 2008 statement, that you saw about 200 civilians there, men and women, almost all Muslims and were able to conclude that they had been removed from their homes and interned there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Of the total number of people interned in Kula prison, the only one who were not Muslims was Vladimir Srebrov and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Vladimir Srebrov is a former SDS official who had a power --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, during the time that you were interrogated, is it correct, as you also explained in your 2008 statement, that you were subjected to physical violence by members of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would say that was the normal procedure with the exception of Tomo Puhalac, an inspector, a former member of the Ministry of the Interior who was extremely fair in his behaviour. As for the others, they just took advantage of the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, at paragraphs 62 through 66 of your statement you refer to Bijeljina and the killings by Arkan and state that -- your belief about whether Dr. Karadzic had anything to do with Arkan's coming to Bijeljina. Now, I take it from the rest of your account of events and your whereabouts that you don't know about any subsequent meetings or contacts between Arkan and Dr. Karadzic or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I know that Fikret Abdic told him that at the time when the barricades were in place that he and Dr. Karadzic were gambling together at Yugoslavia Hotel after the meeting with Mr. Milosevic attended by Dr. Krajisnik and Dr. Koljevic. The case of Bijeljina was a simple case of robbery by a group. In accordance with the information provided to me from the public and state services, the aim was to rob the agricultural bank in Bijeljina that had enormous foreign currency reserves. And a disagreement erupted there between two criminal groups: Arkan and his men on the one hand and a local criminal group on the other. The Presidency decided to send a delegation to resolve the matter. Since they failed in that attempt, then the Presidency instructed me and Delimustafic to go over there and settle it, but that's a long story.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just follow-up on one part of what you just said and that's the reference to what Fikret Abdic told you about Dr. Karadzic's whereabouts at the time of the barricade, which would have been the beginning of March 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 1st of March. I tried to get in touch with him and Koljevic when the barricades were erected, but that this was not exactly properly organised was confirmed by Biljana Plavsic, with whom I spoke about 1.00 in the morning, who had no clue about what was happening and about the barricades. And as for Dr. Krajisnik and Koljevic and the others, none of them was in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's focus for the moment on the -- I just wanted to place the information you were receiving in context by way of date. But as I understand it from what you testified a moment ago and also what you stated in 2002 at page 7, Mr. Abdic told you that when he met with Arkan in Bijeljina at the beginning of April, that Arkan confirmed to him that he, Arkan, had been gambling with Karadzic at the time of the barricades in Sarajevo. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And among other things he used some bad language at the expense of Abdic and his decision to let Izetbegovic head the Presidency instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to the information you received from Mr. Abdic, you also received information, as you explained further in your 2002 statement, from representatives of state security to the same effect. That is, you learned from representatives of state security that Dr. Karadzic was with Arkan gambling at the time of the barricades at the beginning of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: This was the information that our State Security Service received from their counterparts in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about something you said at paragraph 23 of your statement with respect to the mobilisation of large numbers of reserve police officers and members of the BH TO in some municipalities. And you go on to indicate that you took steps to annul such mobilisation orders and recover any weapons. And I gather that was successful because, as you testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, the strength of the reserves did not change from the time you -- during the time of your term in office. And that's found at T -- transcript page 5854 through 55. As you said there: "As far as I know once we came to power we didn't change the strength of the manoeuvre units or the reserve forces, but in agreement with the chiefs of police stations in the field we launched some operational activities concerning staff which -- to the effect that manoeuvre units be better equipped with staff but we didn't change the strength of the manoeuvre unit or the active police forces or, indeed, the reserve forces." And that's a correct recitation of what you stated in --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We did not change it until the session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 11th December 1991. If you wish, I can show you the minutes of that meeting because I have it in my notes. And we proposed that the process of equipping the Ministry of the Interior and the so-called detachment for special operations was something that I was criticised for having spent nearly 60 per cent of the budget. We had information that the war in the former Yugoslavia was supposed to begin in the summer of 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that corroborated some statements made by Mr. Mesic because there was an agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic to split Bosnia between them. We believed that the ministry had to be fully equipped, and for that purpose we ordered American combat helicopters in order to set up this protection detachment that could act as a Rapid Reaction Force and be able to prevent any form of armed conflict and similar activities in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this report and the proposal that was accepted unanimously by the Presidency -- and I purposefully avoided attending that meeting. I sent Branko Kvesic instead because I knew that Nikola Koljevic and all the other members of the Presidency would be there, including Bogic Bogicevic represented the federal Presidency. It seems that without paying much attention the Presidency accepted this and approved our request. I would be the happiest man in the world had this really been accepted and adopted. There would have been no war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For some reason somebody --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've got about -- I think about ten minutes left. I'm going to try to cover -- that's fine. I'm going to try to cover three relatively discrete and short topics. The first one is this: I understand from your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony that you were aware of a training -- police training programme in Croatia that was attended by persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that generally correct? And I'm going to ask you a couple of specific things about that.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That was common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe you clarified in your testimony there that the Bosnian MUP had information that people from Bosnia were applying at "an open competition" at the MUP of Croatia for training slots in a newly opened training centre. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Croatia increased the number of members of Ministry of the Interior, and in my first conversation with the Croatian minister of the interior I said that 400 members from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were there he should compensate me in a way for them. So that was, as I said, common practice to have people from Bosnia-Herzegovina applying to be admitted into the SUP school in Kamenica, in Serbia, or in Croatia. For example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina we had attendees from Montenegro and other parts. Now, after they had increased the number, some 400 members were admitted in -- as one lot and they mostly came from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next topic I wanted to ask you about, which is a couple questions about Mr. Mandic, you stated in your 2002 statement at page 10 that immediately after the dispatch, that is, the Mandic dispatch regarding the MUP, that Mandic and Ostojic participated in an interview on TV and stated that you had a weekend house built or bought by the SDA and it was obvious you should resign. Is it correct that that happened and that was an attempt to discredit you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: It is true that this is what Mandic said. You quoted him correctly. But let me remind you that I had a weekend cottage in Sarajevo in a completely different location. Momcilo Mandic and his younger brother, they were honoured to come and excavate foundations for my house. And then I said, "How come you excavated foundations for that weekend cottage and you don't know where it is located?" And he said, "I was asked to say that." And I thought that it would be inappropriate and unnecessary for me to refute these allegation because we had enough evidence to file criminal reports against Mandic for all that he did in his position as assistant minister, but we didn't go through with that. So in order to avoid any confusion, let me remind you that at the 36th Session of the Serbian republic -- Serbian Assembly in Pale, it was confirmed that I wanted to arrest him and institute criminal proceedings. But allegedly because he made it possible to make payments to policeman of a police station whom I had suspended because of illegal operations. And now, Mr. President, I have to correct you. Your minister of the interior was a criminal and that was the reason why I filed a criminal report against him and why I initiated a procedure to have him removed from the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to risk not coming in under my time when I have an opportunity to do that, so that concludes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. I have to do that because the esteemed Mr. Tieger asked questions making references to various statements, but that is his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us start with the last things that were discussed here. Dr. Zepinic, you said that in an open advertisement for posts, some 400 young men from western Herzegovina applied. In addition to that, did you know about the contingent of several thousand candidates that the SDA had sent to be trained in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is -- Dr. Zepinic has been called as Dr. Karadzic's witness. I don't think it's never too early to remind Dr. Karadzic to refrain from leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll rephrased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the 400 men mostly from western Herzegovina, were they included in the contingent or, rather, do you know that the SDA was sending their candidates to undergo training? Did the SDA send their candidates to Croatia to be trained outside of regular MUP channels?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you misunderstood me. I did not say that 400 candidates applied. I said that they were admitted. I don't know how many of them filed applications. You will have to ask the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia about that. I said that they came from western Herzegovina. But there was some Muslims from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were entitled to file applications. There was no law that could have prevented them from applying to be trained in Skopje, et cetera. The information that you have that some 5.000 people from the SDA were trained, I don't have that kind of information. So please do not advertise the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia and improve their image because they didn't have the capacity to admit so many people. I don't know who gave you this information. I'm telling you that my ministry didn't have it. We had information that among the 400 applicants there was a number of Muslims as well and that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were those men sent by the SDA? By their papers and application papers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That was an open advertisement and anyone was eligible to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D360, please, in e-court. D360.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect I didn't say 5.000. I said "a few thousand." Now, Dr. Zepinic, could you please look at this instruction for candidates signed by Hasan Cengic and it refers to the training of his men at the MUP of Croatia. Did Hasan Cengic play any role?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Hasan Cengic was not an employee of the Ministry of the Interior at all. Who gave him the right to refer to any agreements reached between two Ministries of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are not familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No, and he didn't have the right on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior to invoke any contacts and communications with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Zepinic, did you know where we were staying as the delegation of Bosnian Serbs in Belgrade when we went there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you seem to forget that I was at the head of a service in the Ministry of the Interior. It was only natural, Dr. Karadzic, my friend and colleague, to know every minute detail about your life. I'm sorry for my language, but we had to know how many times a day you visited the lavatory. The ministry had to know with whom you maintained contacts, not only you but everybody else who was in the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Zepinic, this is because I cannot put leading questions to you, can you tell me at which hotel we stayed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: You went to Belgrade so many times, you really expect me to remember everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm asking you about what you heard about Arkan and the gambling. Do you know that in the Intercontinental Hotel there is a casino as well?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I am not interested in that. I'm just conveying what I heard from Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you what kind of gambling could involve only two persons?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, your question is unfair. I'm telling you again this information was given me by Mr. Fikret Abdic and he heard it on the barricades when he met with Arkan. Whether there was roulette, whether you played poker, whether there were five or ten of you is beside the point, and the ministry is not interested in that. It was interested in knowing where members of the nationalist parties and Presidency were at the time when the barricades were erected. And why was this hot potato given to the ministry and Dr. Zepinic and the only one who offered some assistance was Biljana Plavsic. Neither Izetbegovic, Ganic, Kljujic, you, or anyone else who could influence the events related to the barricade responded to my pleas. That is what we were interested in. Whether you were really gambling and losing money, that was not our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said today that I knew about your mother. Unfortunately, I heard about that during the proofing session. Can you please tell us how your mother died, was she killed or ...?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: She had a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from me that you should be arrested and killed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it from you. All I'm saying is that there was this information floating around, but you yourself never said that. I must even admit that in certain situations you tried to protect me and defend me from the extremists in your party and my principles of neutrality. You said that it was difficult to remove Vito than Tito simply because there were no arguments to initiate any proceedings against me. You never said to me, at least not publicly that I should be killed, but the service provided me with the information that there were seven attempts on my life and there was no indication that the SDS was behind them except in one instance involving Kerovic when we went to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, is it a fact -- what did you say about Kerovic and Bijeljina? But you believed that I knew nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I'm more than certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your commitment to the brotherhood and unity, was it something that was secret or did you publicly proclaim that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, in all my speeches and public appearances I advocated the brotherhood of unity to remain in our country, and I didn't see any reason for that not to happen. I cannot separate what I thought in private or in public. That was my general commitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I know what your political position was when we nominated you to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were quite clear about my position and you can see from my statement that I explained how it came about. And I also mentioned that due to that you were exposed to pressure from the Assembly of the SDS not to accept my nomination, but you opposed these kind of views because you simply said that you want a person of authority and a professional in that position, a person who will not side with any political party. And I really must reiterate that you never insisted on my becoming a member of the SDS because obviously you knew that I would never agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have an opportunity of seeing what my attitude was towards others or, more specifically, let me ask you this way. Did you and I take part in the selection of the head of the regional MUP in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. If you remember, we had this painstaking conversation, six hours long, because people were pressuring you to take another candidate, whereas I was in favour of keeping Stojan Zupljanin who was the head of the CSB from before. I knew him personally from sports. He had a degree in law. There was no reason to dismiss him. We did discuss that specifically. And I know that Banja Luka never forgave you for that because you agreed to have my candidate, if I can put it that way, stay on rather than the candidate that was proposed by the SDS for the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm so glad that you remember that. On pages 74 and 75 the learned Mr. Tieger asked you to confirm whether I was counting on the support of the JNA. This is what I would like to ask you: On the whole, what was the SDS in favour of in terms of the state as such?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, that requires a longer elaboration, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just in relation to Yugoslavia, if I may ask him.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can put it this way, you kept changing your positions, all three parties. In the beginning, before the elections, the national parties clearly said that they would preserve the brotherhood and unity that was there and that there would not be a conflict at all. I would like to remind you of your statement, Dr. Karadzic, when you said if Durakovic wins, there's going to be war. If Izetbegovic wins, we are going to seek agreement; is that correct? I'm going to remind you of your statement that you made when you were the president of the green party, when you said communism is a bad thing but nationalism is even worse. When speaking about Yugoslavia, we have to look at that from another point of view. What does Yugoslavia mean? What does the Rump Yugoslavia mean? Tito's Yugoslavia had to go through certain forms of transformation because the overall world situation called for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. But let us be specific. Which programme of mine would have been supported by the JNA? What did I think was the case, the programme of preserving Yugoslavia or the programme of secession and of splitting up Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
